walkthroughs.body_html:
An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of instructions that solves a problem. A recipe is an algorithm: list ingredients (inputs), follow steps in order, produce a cake (output).

Algorithms must be unambiguous and terminate (eventually stop).

Pseudocode uses keywords like IF, WHILE, OUTPUT. Flowcharts use shapes: ovals for start/end, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions.

Both describe the same algorithm in different forms.

Abstraction: a Tube map ignores real distances — only stations and lines matter.

Decomposition: building a game means splitting it into graphics, input, scoring and sound sub-problems.

mcqs.q: Is an algorithm the same thing as a computer program?
options: No - an algorithm is the abstract sequence of steps; a program is one implementation of it in a particular language. The same algorithm can be coded many ways.
Yes - algorithms only exist once they are typed into a computer.
Yes - only the arrows matter, the shapes are decoration.
Yes - algorithm is just the formal word for program code.

mcqs.q: Does an IF statement repeat its block of code?
options: Yes - algorithms only exist once they are typed into a computer.
Yes - IF keeps running its block until the condition turns false.
No - IF is selection: it decides once whether to execute the block; repetition needs an iteration construct such as WHILE or FOR.
Yes - IF and WHILE are interchangeable keywords.

mcqs.q: Do flowchart symbols mean whatever the author wants?
options: Yes - only the arrows matter, the shapes are decoration.
No - the symbols are standardised: ovals for start/end, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions, parallelograms for input/output.
Yes - algorithms only exist once they are typed into a computer.
Yes - any shape can represent any kind of step.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Sequence”?
options: A diagram of an algorithm using standard symbols - ovals for start and end, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions - linked by arrows.
Instructions executed one after another in the exact order they are written - the most basic structure of any algorithm.
Repeating a group of steps, either a fixed number of times or while a condition remains true, instead of writing them out repeatedly.
Choosing between alternative paths through an algorithm depending on whether a condition is true or false, such as an if-else.
